chapter: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
title: Mal Hallett and union pressure
summary: Playing at the Palace Theatre with Mal Hallett, who agreed to pay scale to protect him from Glaser's cut.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: So what happened was that... Heh-heh. I went on my tour. I was going up to play for Scribner(?). He's the one who used to book all the bands in New England. And I played a date with Mal Hallett's band.

No, but I had my little band. When I came to New York, the band stayed up there working. They used Max Kaminsky, heh-heh, and my brother and them, they used to let him go to the bar and get a drink while they played, because he couldn't keep up with them. Heh-heh.
So anyhow, I came to New York, which was the first White band I worked with, really.

Yeah, at the Palace Theatre. And he said... I told him, "Boy I got this wire from the union that says if I don't go sign up with Glaser, then I can't work. They will tear up my card." Well, that's politics, you know that. So Mal said, "Well, I'm going to tell what I'm going to do. I'll pay you what I'm supposed to pay you, but if

they want to know, I'll just tell them that you only got scale, so they can't (?) your scale." So that kept them from taking any money from me. So I stayed on for a while, and finally, you know, the (?) came back and broke the band up.
